body.heading: Surfaces that catch on each other
paragraphs: No surface is perfectly smooth. Under a microscope, even polished metal is a landscape of tiny peaks and valleys, and when two surfaces press together those peaks catch, stick and tear apart as the surfaces slide. That resistance to sliding is friction, and it always acts opposite to the movement — or the attempted movement.

Friction comes in two strengths. Static friction holds still objects in place and adjusts itself up to a limit; it is what keeps a parked car from rolling and a book from sliding off a tilted desk. Once sliding starts, kinetic friction takes over, usually a little weaker, which is why a heavy box is hardest to get moving and slightly easier to keep moving.

body.heading: The force you cannot live without
paragraphs: Walking, driving and holding a pencil all depend on friction. Your shoe grips the ground so the ground can push you forward; a car's tyres grip the road so the car can accelerate, steer and brake. Brake pads work by deliberately creating huge friction, turning the car's movement energy into heat.

A match lights because friction between the match head and the striking strip generates enough heat in one quick scrape to start a chemical reaction. Climbers, gymnasts and weightlifters dust their hands with chalk for the same reason in reverse: more grip, more friction, fewer slips.

body.heading: The force engineers fight
paragraphs: Inside engines and machines, friction is mostly an enemy. It wastes energy as heat, wears surfaces down and can overheat moving parts. Engineers fight it with smooth bearings, careful design and lubricants — oil or grease that keeps a thin film between surfaces so they slide on liquid instead of grinding on each other.

The trick is balance. A hovercraft floats on air to escape friction almost entirely, while a Formula 1 tyre is engineered for maximum stickiness. Friction is neither good nor bad: it is a tool, and skilled design means having exactly as much of it as the job requires.

description: Friction stops your feet slipping and wears out machine parts — the same force is both the hero and the villain.
